🔖In a tweet, Ghalibaf preemptively dismissed today's much-hyped decision by the US central bank on interest rates as inconsequential regardless of its outcome, writing:

📌Let's see whether the Federal Reserve can open the Strait of Hormuz or produce even one more barrel of oil by raising interest rates?!

📌You can't manage (anchor) inflation expectations in America by raising and lowering interest rates, because those expectations are driven by the supply-side shock caused by the blockage of energy chokepoints — namely the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and have nothing to do with interest rates. It is the "Strait of Hormuz risk" that determines the rate, and control over that risk now lies with Iran.

📌Ghalibaf's emphasis in this post is on the idea that the era of managing inflation and inflation expectations using demand-side tools alone (interest rates) is over, and that it is geopolitics that now holds the upper hand in shaping economic indicators such as inflation.

📌Under normal conditions, a central bank traditionally seeks to anchor inflation expectations to its inflation target or to a credible long-term inflation rate in order to contain inflation, and it achieves this anchoring by adjusting interest rates in line with the inflation target and the economy's distance from full capacity.

📌But in this post, the Parliament Speaker, by upending the classic formula for setting interest rates in America, warns market participants that tinkering with interest rates will not achieve the goal of containing inflation in America, and that they must factor new variables into their calculations — such as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and accept that circumstances have changed: unless Iran wills it, inflation expectations in America will not be anchorable, and inflation will keep climbing.

🔰 The "Oman Trap" Sanitized by the Government News Agency!

🔸 The news coverage and analysis of recent diplomatic maneuvers has once again laid bare the dangerous naivety of certain domestic factions in the face of the complex designs of the Western-Arab front.

🔸 At a time when the sudden cancellation or postponement of the Salalah meeting in Oman — at America's direct dictation to Riyadh and its allies — proved that these meetings are not meant for convergence, but are rather a pre-planned trap to "blunt the sharp edge of Iran's weapon, namely its authority over the Strait of Hormuz," the strange insistence and eagerness of the "government news agency" to once again pave the way for this snare is deeply worthy of reflection.

🔸 The government news agency, in a piece penned by one of its former diplomats, ignoring the hostile nature of the other side's game, has claimed: "Fortunately, the formation of this meeting... is the demand of all Persian Gulf regional countries, and it has been postponed, not suspended; therefore, the likelihood of this meeting being held is very high." This passive approach is being pumped out while numerous historical experiences have shown that retreating from Iran's leverage tools in the Persian Gulf only makes the Western side more brazen in its hostile designs.

🔸 The author of this piece, which has been republished in the official government media, ignoring the conspiratorial nature of the cancellation of this meeting, insists that "to achieve this goal, holding the summit in Oman is a vital necessity, and these countries are advised to arrange for its formation as soon as possible, because it is a new opportunity."

🔸 This level of eagerness to play on the field of a region whose control room is located in Washington completes the enemy's psychological operation. By giving orders to its regional subordinates and canceling the Salalah meeting, America practically showed that it is not seeking any sustainable regional mechanism and only intends to limit Iran's instruments of influence through diplomatic corridors.

🔸 In another part of this piece, turning a blind eye to the main goals of the American-Zionist enemy, it states: "Recent developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, as well as Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea, have proven that security in these two regions cannot be established by foreign powers."

🔸 Although disappointment with the enemy is a positive step, the government media's renewed excitement to once again spread the same trap that was once disrupted by the Western-Arab axis will inflict irreparable damage on the components of national authority. The time has come for the country's official media, instead of pinning hopes on the mirage of formal meetings, to focus on preserving and strengthening Iran's field-level levers of authority.

Criticism of officials on State TV is not a big problem, but on the condition that it is not one-sided. And secondly, the person being criticized should be given the opportunity to defend themselves and provide the necessary explanations. ◀️ In general, State TV should have its comprehensiveness and should not be in the hands of a particular group so that they, according to their own desires, endorse some individuals, strengthen some individuals, and conversely, suppress others. He stressed that Oman remains committed to strengthening dialogues that contribute to "sustainable stability and cooperation in the region." Abbas Araghchi, the Foreign Minister of the Islamic Republic, had previously said he would attend the eight-party meeting of foreign ministers from the coastal countries of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman in Salalah on Monday. The meeting was supposed to discuss a plan by Iran and Oman to establish a mechanism for the safe passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz. The postponement comes as the United States had previously emphasized that it would not take part in negotiations related to the Strait of Hormuz and would focus any direct talks with the Islamic Republic on the nuclear file. American officials have told regional countries that Washington will not negotiate over the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, and that the main subject of any potential negotiations with Tehran should be the Islamic Republic's nuclear program. Marco Rubio, the U.S. Secretary of State, had also previously said that the Strait of Hormuz should not be under the control of the Islamic Republic, and that the United States would act to guarantee the security of shipping along this route. In contrast, the Islamic Republic and Oman have sought to bring regional countries into dialogue about a mechanism for ship passage through the Strait of Hormuz. The results of Tehran and Muscat's consultations on safe shipping routes were supposed to be presented to the regional countries at this meeting. @VahidHeadline 📡 @VahidOnline
